With matching inputs the two programs agree to about 6.1e-5, so the gap below comes from input data, not from the flash. With DWSIM's own data the separator vapour carries 2.842 mol % NH₃ against the engine's 2.555 mol %, and the H₂ and N₂ dissolved in the liquid differ by a factor of about 1.7 and 3.4. Dissolved N₂ follows the N₂–NH₃ kij, which the engine sets to zero; dissolved H₂ follows how H₂ is represented (effective or true critical constants); the NH₃ in the vapour moves with both, in opposite directions. This comparison does not show which set is closer to a real loop; for loop work, check these numbers against plant separator data.

7 · Three-phase (VLLE) and liquid–liquid flash

The three-phase separator, and every flash when the method's valid phases include a second liquid, tests the two-phase answer for another liquid (Michelsen tangent-plane distance), converges vapour, light liquid and heavy liquid with a three-phase Rachford–Rice, and keeps the state with the lowest Gibbs energy. 12 · Kinetic plug-flow and CSTR reactors vs exact solutions

Power-law kinetics in the chosen phase of the property method. The plug-flow reactor integrates molar flows and enthalpy flow (Dormand–Prince RK5(4), switching to the L-stable Rosenbrock method RODAS3 when the kinetics are stiff); the CSTR solves the extents and temperature by Newton from several starts, reports every steady state it finds, and takes very fast kinetics to the steady state by pseudo-transient continuation. References: Levenspiel's closed forms for first-order reactions with volume change, scipy LSODA and root-bracketing on the same ideal-gas balances (adiabatic, cooled and fixed-duty reactors, including all three steady states of an exothermic CSTR), the closed-form solution of a linear system with a stiffness ratio of 3·10⁶, and the NIST-JANAF water-gas-shift equilibrium for reactors whose reverse rate comes from the equilibrium constant.

13 · Catalytic (LHHW / Hougen–Watson) rate laws

Rates of the form k(T)·[Π aorder − reverse]/(Σ Kt(T) Π ae)m, with a thermodynamically consistent driving force when the reverse rate comes from the equilibrium constant (the databank's or your own ln K correlation). References: the closed-form Langmuir–Hinshelwood plug-flow and stirred-tank solutions, and the published Xu & Froment (1989) steam-reforming model — three reversible reactions with negative hydrogen orders and a squared adsorption term — integrated independently with scipy, isothermal and adiabatic.

14 · Vapour association of carboxylic acids

With an activity-coefficient method, acids dimerise in the vapour (chemical theory: ideal gas of monomers, dimers and cross dimers). The measured vapour pressure and heat of vaporisation refer to this associated vapour, so the liquid enthalpy built from them is now consistent with the formation enthalpies — without association it is about 28 kJ/mol too high for acetic acid, which made liquid heats of reaction and adiabatic temperatures wrong. References: NIST liquid enthalpies of formation, the DIPPR vapour-pressure equation, and an independently written chemical-theory solution for vapour compressibilities.

15 · CO₂ absorption in aqueous MEA

The aqueous-MEA method solves the carbamate (2 MEA + CO₂ ⇌ MEAH⁺ + MEACOO⁻) and bicarbonate (MEA + CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ MEAH⁺ + HCO₃⁻) equilibria of the published Akula et al. model as implemented in the open-source IDAES process-modelling framework; CO₂ follows Henry's law on the free molecular CO₂ (N₂O analogy), water and MEA Raoult's law on the true species. Enthalpies come from the temperature dependence of the same fugacities, so the heat of absorption is consistent with the solubility. References: the IDAES property-package test values, an independent scipy solution of the published equations, and the IDAES heat of absorption.

Against measured vapour pressures

Total pressure over 30 wt % MEA (7.017 mol/kg water) measured by Arshad et al. (J. Chem. Eng. Data 59, 2014, 764; NIST ThermoML), against the engine's bubble pressure. At 120 °C the model is within 2 % up to a loading of 0.32 mol/mol and then over-predicts more and more (+19 % at 0.40, +37 % at 0.44); at 80 °C it is within 10 % to 0.44, and at 40 °C within 20 % at 0.5. Above about 0.55 it over-predicts the CO₂ pressure about twofold — a known limit of ideal-solution chemical-equilibrium models. In a regenerator this makes CO₂ look slightly easier to strip at the rich end, so reboiler duties come out somewhat low.

The pitzer.dat KHCO₃ parameters are fitted to about 3 mol/kg. In strong, highly converted solutions they make the model thermodynamically unstable (a spurious liquid–liquid split) close to where KHCO₃ would in fact crystallise; the engine maps that onset over 0–250 °C and, past 95 % of it, holds the properties at the boundary and extrapolates smoothly (the stream report flags such states). PHREEQC evaluates those states without a stability check, so they are listed separately and not graded — all are cold or 40 wt % solutions converted 60–90 % to bicarbonate, beyond normal hot-carbonate practice:

At high concentration the Pitzer water activity falls below the handbook's 20 °C vapour pressures (−8 % at 46 wt %) and the heat capacity of 40 wt % solution is 10 % low; between 20 and 30 wt % — the Benfield range — both agree within 1–4 %. The Pitzer parameters carry fitted temperature terms to about 90–100 °C and are extrapolated above that. Promoters (DEA, glycine, vanadium) change absorption rates, not the equilibrium, and are represented through tray efficiencies.

17 · Murphree tray efficiency

A tray with Murphree vapour efficiency E leaves its vapour at y = yin + E(K x − yin) instead of in equilibrium; the efficiency can be set for every tray or per component. Reference: the exact solution of the tray equations for a dilute absorber with a straight equilibrium line (numpy), which equals the Lewis–Kremser closed form. The regenerator case checks the condenser-temperature specification used for amine and carbonate strippers.

Scope

These checks verify the implementation against independent references. Agreement with another simulator shows the equations are solved correctly for the given parameters; it does not make a property method suitable for every system — Peng–Robinson without fitted kij over-predicts the solubility of water in hydrocarbon liquids, ChemSep NRTL / UNIQUAC parameters are fitted to vapour–liquid data, and the urea units remain empirical correlations. Use the results for preliminary engineering and confirm them against plant data before design use. Kinetic reactors are only as good as the rate expressions entered, and the acid association model covers dimerisation only (no acid–water cross association; binary parameters fitted without association may need refitting). The CO₂ packages cover CO₂ only (no H₂S, NH₃ or MDEA / activated MDEA chemistry), and tray efficiencies stand in for rate-based mass transfer. The inputs for every case above are in the engine test set, cases MB-089 to MB-195.
